sections.heading: Coming to you with no excuses
sections.text:
God, you are greater than I can understand or measure. When I stand before you honestly, I have nothing to brag about. Apart from your mercy, I am empty, guilty, and dying.

My sin has cost me more than I can repair. It has put me outside the favor I was made to enjoy, damaged your image in me, driven me from your presence, and left me exposed to the judgment your law rightly pronounces. I cannot rescue myself. If deliverance depends on me, I have no hope.
theological_themes: God’s unsearchable greatness and holiness
Human sin, guilt, and spiritual helplessness
The law’s just condemnation of sin
The need for salvation from outside the self

scripture_references.connection: Paul explains that God’s law silences human boasting and makes sin known rather than providing a way for sinners to justify themselves. This supports the prayer’s honest confession that self-rescue is impossible.
This passage describes the natural human condition as spiritually dead and under wrath apart from God’s intervention. It grounds the prayer’s language of helplessness and exposure to judgment.

sections.heading: Receiving the rescue you planned before I wanted it
sections.text:
But you have not left me there. The answer is in you, not in me.

Before I deserved anything, before I even wanted you rightly, you had already planned a rescue that displays your wisdom, justice, mercy, and glory. This salvation is so deep and beautiful that even angels long to understand it more fully.

And you have not kept it far away. Through your Word, you bring the good news close. You call me, invite me, and urge me to come to you.
theological_themes: God’s gracious initiative in salvation
The eternal plan of redemption in Christ
The gospel as God’s near and urgent invitation
Salvation that glorifies God’s character

scripture_references.connection: Paul presents salvation as God’s gracious purpose in Christ, planned before the foundation of the world and carried out for the praise of his glory. This directly supports the prayer’s emphasis on an everlasting plan that begins in God, not in human merit.
Peter says the prophets searched into the grace now announced in the gospel and that angels long to look into these things. This illuminates the prayer’s wonder at the depth of God’s saving plan.
Paul says the message of faith is near and calls people to trust and call on the Lord for salvation. This supports the prayer’s claim that God’s Word comes close and invites the sinner to Christ.

sections.heading: Finding all my help in Jesus and his cross
sections.text:
So let me come as I really am: convinced of my sin and done pretending I can save myself.

Let me find Jesus to be the power of God for my salvation. Let his death be the place where my fear, guilt, and helplessness meet your mercy. Let the cross be the center of my relief and the fountain of every blessing you give through the gospel.
theological_themes: Christ as the only Savior
The cross as the center of salvation
Relief from guilt and judgment through Christ’s death
Gospel blessings flowing from the atonement

scripture_references.connection: Paul identifies Christ crucified as God’s power and wisdom to those who are being saved. This supports the prayer’s request to find Jesus as the power of God for salvation.
Paul teaches that God reconciles all things to himself through the blood of Christ’s cross. This grounds the prayer’s focus on Christ’s death as the source of true relief and gospel blessing.

sections.heading: Letting the cross reshape what I love
sections.text:
Bring me again and again to the cross. By it, loosen my grip on the world and the world’s grip on me.

There, teach me humility. Give me reasons to be patient when life is hard, and strength to deny myself when my desires pull me away from you. Make me generous and ready to do good. Give me faith that holds tightly to eternal life, hope that lifts my head when I am low, and love that binds me forever to Jesus—the one who died for me and rose again.
theological_themes: Union with Christ in his death and resurrection
Dying to the world’s claims
Humility, patience, self-denial, love, and hope shaped by the cross
Faith laying hold of eternal life

scripture_references.connection: Paul says the cross of Christ has crucified the world to him and him to the world. This directly supports the prayer’s desire for the cross to sever worldly allegiance.

Paul teaches that Christ’s death and resurrection reorient believers so they no longer live for themselves but for him. This grounds the prayer’s movement from receiving Christ’s death to living in self-denial and love.
Peter connects Christ’s resurrection with a living hope and an imperishable inheritance. This supports the prayer’s request for hope and faith that reach toward eternal life.

sections.heading: Letting Christ’s blood change my everyday life
sections.text:
Because Jesus shed his blood for me, make me more grateful for every mercy you give.

When you correct me, keep me humble instead of resentful. Make me more eager to serve you, more alert when temptation is near, more at peace with the circumstances you have assigned to me, and more useful to the people around me.

Let the mercy that saved me become the mercy that changes me.
theological_themes: Christ’s atonement producing gratitude and holiness
God’s fatherly correction
Watchfulness against temptation
Contentment under providence
Usefulness in loving service to others

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews presents God’s discipline as the loving correction of a Father who trains his children for holiness. This supports the prayer’s request to be humble under God’s correction rather than hardened by it.

Paul says God’s saving grace trains believers to reject ungodliness and become zealous for good works. This fits the prayer’s desire that Christ’s redeeming work produce watchfulness, service, and practical holiness.
Paul speaks of learning contentment in varied circumstances through Christ’s strength. This supports the prayer’s request to become more content where God has placed me.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses strong Reformed/Puritan language about sin forfeiting God’s favor, stripping the divine image, banishment from God’s presence, and exposure to the curse of the law. These themes are biblically grounded but doctrinally weighty, so the modern version preserves their seriousness without softening them.

The phrase “without my desert or desire” reflects God’s initiative in salvation before human merit or rightly ordered desire. This can touch contested debates about divine sovereignty and human response; the adaptation keeps the emphasis on grace without expanding into a full doctrinal system.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Stripped me of thy image” was rendered as “damaged your image in me,” because historic Christian theology usually understands the image of God as marred by sin rather than utterly erased.

“Repair to that cross” was adapted as “bring me again and again to the cross,” meaning not a repeated sacrifice of Christ but a repeated return of faith, repentance, and dependence to the once-for-all work of Christ.

“His death the centre of all relief” was interpreted broadly as relief from guilt, fear, helplessness, and judgment, while keeping the cross as the source rather than shifting the focus to general emotional comfort.
